abstract.p: Conspicuous tropical fishes are readily detected by sea users, but repeated sightings and uncertain identifications can distort occurrence histories. We reviewed source-traceable Mediterranean records of Paracanthurus hepatus and Heniochus intermedius through 1 October 2026 and documented two additional video observations: P. hepatus at Cap Dramont, France, on 10 September 2024, and Heniochus cf. intermedius near Sorrento, Italy, on 23 June 2026. Five P. hepatus observation episodes represent at least four individuals. The French observation was approximately 79 m from the site of a fish removed in July and 0.92 km from another individual last observed five days earlier; it may represent the latter fish after displacement or an additional individual. The reconciled Heniochus chronology contains 27 reported occurrence entries across 11 countries: 14 retained as H. intermedius and 13 as H. cf. intermedius. Aquarium release is the leading hypothesis for P. hepatus, whereas Suez Canal dispersal is plausible for H. intermedius; individual pathways remain unverified. Source reconciliation and conservative identification improve citizen-science contributions to Mediterranean biodiversity monitoring.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: The Mediterranean Sea is one of the most intensively invaded marine regions worldwide, and its non-indigenous fish fauna reflects several fundamentally different introduction pathways. The Suez Canal dominates the arrival of Indo-Pacific fishes naturally occurring in the Red Sea, while shipping, aquaculture and aquarium-related releases account for a smaller but ecologically important fraction of introductions that cannot be explained by unaided natural dispersal [1,2,3]. For fishes, pathway attribution is particularly informative when native-range geography either provides or excludes a plausible natural corridor. Contrasting species with different native distributions can therefore help separate the process of arrival from the environmental conditions that subsequently determine persistence and establishment.

The palette surgeonfish Paracanthurus hepatus (Linnaeus, 1766) is a tropical, reef-associated acanthurid native to the Indo-Pacific, from eastern Africa and the Mascarene region eastwards to the central Pacific, but it is absent from the Red Sea [4,5]. It is exceptionally recognizable because of its bright blue body, black palette-like pattern and yellow caudal fin and is among the best-known marine ornamental fishes. In the European Union, an estimated 26 million marine ornamental fishes were imported between 2014 and 2021, while species-level information was unavailable for roughly one third of imported specimens [6]. The first Mediterranean occurrence of P. hepatus was documented at Bat Yam, Israel, from a single individual observed in 2015 [7]. Subsequent records came from Corsica in 2021 and eastern Provence in 2024 [5,8,9]. That study presented its record as the first for the western Mediterranean [5], although the earlier Corsican occurrence [8,9] indicates that this was not the case. Because P. hepatus is naturally absent from the Red Sea, aquarium release or another direct human-mediated introduction is far more plausible than Lessepsian migration. The publication history of P. hepatus also illustrates a broader problem in invasion biogeography. Conspicuous organisms can be detected rapidly through divers, fishers and citizen-science networks, whereas formal publication may occur years later [10]. Later papers may consequently describe an event as a regional first even when an earlier validated observation exists in grey literature or monitoring databases. Curated occurrence datasets such as ORMEF were developed to reconcile scattered records, dates and sources and to reduce such inconsistencies [11]. For rare fishes, repeated observations of the same individual create an additional risk of inflating occurrence counts unless records are reconciled at individual or episode level.

A contrasting case is provided by the Red Sea bannerfish Heniochus intermedius Steindachner, 1893, a chaetodontid native to the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. Its first Mediterranean record dates to 2002 in Türkiye [12], followed by records from Lebanon, Israel, Malta, Türkiye, Egypt, Syria and additional localities [13,14,15,16,17,18]. A recent critical synthesis reassessed Mediterranean Heniochus occurrences and added six H. intermedius or H. cf. intermedius observations from 2021 to 2025, including video-only records from Italy, Cyprus and Greece [19]. That study also reported the first confirmed Mediterranean Heniochus acuminatus (Linnaeus, 1758), from Cyprus, demonstrating that more than one congener can occur in the basin and that video-only identifications require caution [19]. A 2024 Adriatic video initially assigned only to Heniochus sp. was subsequently considered compatible with H. cf. intermedius [19,20]. Diagnostic treatments of western Indian Ocean chaetodontids provide the morphological framework for discriminating these congeners [21].

Here, we use these two conspicuous tropical fishes (H. intermedius and P. hepatus) as contrasting case studies of Mediterranean biodiversity change. We (1) document the new French and Italian video observations and assess individual identity and taxonomic confidence; (2) place these observations within published Mediterranean occurrence histories, updating the recent Heniochus synthesis with specific source corrections and additional reports; and (3) compare potential introduction pathways and regional establishment status, identifying priorities for subsequent monitoring.

sec.title: 2.1. Literature and Occurrence-Data Review
sec.p: A targeted literature review was updated through 1 October 2026 using web searches and reference backtracking. Search terms combined Paracanthurus hepatus or P. hepatus with Mediterranean, Israel, Bat Yam, France, Corsica, Ajaccio, Provence, Saint-Raphaël, Cap Dramont and aquarium release. For Heniochus, terms included Heniochus intermedius, Heniochus cf. intermedius, Heniochus acuminatus and Heniochus sp., combined with Mediterranean and the countries or localities represented in Table 1, particularly Syria and Sorrento. Peer-reviewed papers were prioritized, with the CIESM Atlas [4], the French institutional monitoring report [8] and the French ichthyological synthesis [9] providing additional context or occurrence evidence. The 2026 regional review [19] was the principal event-level Heniochus baseline through November 2025; its table and cited primary papers were compared to identify duplicate entries, coordinate discrepancies and omitted records. Searches also targeted observations after that baseline. This was a targeted source reconciliation, not a systematic review or an independent census of occurrence databases; completeness is limited by source accessibility, indexing and reporting.

A record was included when its locality and date or year were traceable to a primary publication or institutional report and its evidence type could be established. Evidence included collected specimens, photographs, videos and visual observations explicitly retained by Azzurro et al. (2026) [19]. Repeated observations attributed by their source to the same fish were consolidated as one episode. Separate reported events were retained when individual identity was unresolved, without assuming that each represented a distinct fish. Geographic coordinates were reproduced or converted from original sources when recoverable; regional-review positions were used otherwise and marked separately. Locality-only observations and a fish-market record were mapped using approximate locator symbols rather than asserted capture coordinates. Coordinate provenance is retained in Table 1. Taxonomic assignments follow Azzurro et al. (2026) [19] where applicable, with original source names given in Table 1; historical vouchers were not independently re-examined. Newly recovered records retain their original published identification.

sec.title: 2.2. Paracanthurus hepatus Late-Season Observation and Spatial Comparison
sec.p: On 10 September 2024 at approximately 17:30, a single P. hepatus was filmed near Cap Dramont, Saint-Raphaël, France (43.4098627° N, 6.8454437° E). The fish was visually estimated at 20–25 cm total length and occurred over the red volcanic rocky reef of the Estérel massif, in the presence of Chromis chromis, Oblada melanura, Diplodus spp. and labrid fishes (Labridae). The individual approached the observer and showed little avoidance. A still frame extracted from the video was used for documentation (Figure 1a).

The position of this observation was compared with the two eastern Provence individuals reported by Boudouresque et al. [5]. Their Individual No. 1 was recorded below the Dramont semaphore near Île d’Or at 43°24.561′ N, 6°50.767′ E (43.409350° N, 6.846117° E), and was speared in July 2024. Individual No. 2 was observed at 43°24.666′ N, 6°51.402′ E (43.411100° N, 6.856700° E), between 14 July and 5 September 2024. Great-circle distances between these coordinates and the 10 September observation were calculated with the haversine formula.

sec.title: 2.3. Heniochus Video Observation and Taxonomic Assessment
sec.p: On 23 June 2026, a single Heniochus was recorded on underwater video during spearfishing activity in the Sorrento area, Campania, southern Tyrrhenian Sea, Italy. The reported depth was approximately 8 m and water temperature were 27 °C; the measurement method and calibration were not available. Exact geographic coordinates were 40.65862° N, 14.39784° E. Three original video sequences and the supplied screenshot were considered in conjunction with the diagnostic treatment of Heniochus [21] and the conservative identification approach used for recent Mediterranean video records [19]. The screenshot is reproduced unchanged in Figure 1b. No specimen was retained, and diagnostic meristic counts and fine morphological characters could not be assessed, although the overall colour pattern appears more consistent with H. intermedius. This species typically exhibits yellowish ventral body colouration and an anterior black band reaching the posterior margin of the eye, whereas H. acuminatus generally has a predominantly white body and an anterior body band situated farther behind the eye. Consequently, the Sorrento fish is reported as H. cf. intermedius.

sec.title: 3.1. Paracanthurus hepatus: Verified Mediterranean Chronology
sec.p: The review recovered five substantiated observation episodes from three Mediterranean sectors and two countries between 2015 and 2024 (Table 2; Figure 2). No additional substantiated Mediterranean occurrence after the September 2024 Provence cluster was located in the sources searched up to 1 October 2026. The five episodes correspond to a minimum of four distinct fish; the number represented by these five episodes may be five if the 10 September 2024 observation represents an individual different from the fish monitored at Cap Dramont until 5 September.

sec.p: The earliest record was the single fish documented at Bat Yam, Israel, in 2015 and published by Marcelli et al. [7]. The next confirmed geographic occurrence was in Corsica on 21 August 2021 at Isolella–I Setti Navi, Gulf of Ajaccio (41.8450° N, 8.748333° E). The Réseau Alien Corse recorded an isolated individual that remained observable in the area for several weeks [8]. This was the first documented occurrence from French Mediterranean waters and, chronologically, the first substantiated western Mediterranean record. Its later peer-reviewed treatment in Iglésias et al. [9] confirms the importance of incorporating validated grey literature when reconstructing first occurrences.

The 2024 eastern Provence cluster involved at least two distinct individuals. Individual No. 1 of Boudouresque et al. [5], approximately 20 cm long, was observed at about 5 m depth over a rocky reef and was speared in July. Individual No. 2, also estimated at approximately 20 cm, was repeatedly observed from 14 July to 5 September at 1–5 m depth over Posidonia oceanica meadow and rocky reef. During approximately 20 days of directed tracking in mid-August to early September, that fish was considered relatively sedentary within a roughly 40 m diameter area. Tracking ended because of severe weather and the fish was not found afterward.

sec.title: 3.2. Paracanthurus hepatus: The 10 September 2024 Cap Dramont Observation
sec.p: The fish filmed on 10 September 2024 showed the diagnostic blue-and-black body pattern and yellow caudal fin of P. hepatus (Figure 1a). The estimated total length of 20–25 cm is comparable to, or slightly larger than, the ~20 cm estimated for each of the two individuals previously reported from the same coastal sector [5]. Its coordinates were approximately 79 m from the site where Individual No. 1 had been speared in July, but identity with that fish is impossible because the latter had been removed. Conversely, the 10 September position was approximately 0.92 km from the site used by Individual No. 2 through 5 September (Figure 2, eastern Provence enlargement). The new observation therefore has two plausible interpretations: it represents Individual No. 2 at a position roughly 0.9 km from its previously reported location, or it documents an additional individual not previously recognized. The low avoidance shown by the filmed fish is consistent with the tolerance of close approach (to about 1 m) reported for Individual No. 2 [5], but this is only weak supporting evidence of identity. No individual tracking data establish either displacement or a causal role of the intervening severe weather.

sec.title: 3.3. Heniochus intermedius and H. cf. intermedius: Mediterranean Chronology and the Sorrento Observation
sec.p: The original Sorrento footage supports assignment to Heniochus through the deep, laterally compressed body, elongated dorsal filament and banded colour pattern (Figure 1b). The visible pattern is compatible with H. intermedius, but water colour, viewing angle, resolution and incomplete visibility of diagnostic characters limit discrimination from similar congeners, including H. acuminatus [19,21]. We therefore retain the conservative designation H. cf. intermedius. This is a provisional attribution, not a confirmed species-level identification or evidence that every Mediterranean video-only Heniochus belongs to the same species.

The updated occurrence account contains 27 reported Mediterranean entries through 1 October 2026, distributed across 11 countries (Table 1; Figure 2). Fourteen entries retain a species-level assignment to H. intermedius, while 13 are treated as H. cf. intermedius. These are occurrence entries, not an estimate of 27 distinct fish: repeat sightings explicitly attributed to one individual are consolidated, and the first Antalya episode included a sighted pair with one subsequent capture [12,13]. Azzurro et al. (2026) [19] provide the baseline occurrences, the published taxonomic reassessments and six new reports from 2021 to 2025. Our update consolidates the two Egyptian rows into one original event and adds the Banyas [23], Latakia [25] and Sorrento reports. It is a targeted update of that synthesis.

The two Egyptian rows in the regional review were consolidated because the primary account reports one photographed fish captured on 16 November 2017 [17]. Two additional Syrian reports were recovered: the 21 May 2022 Banyas specimen [23] and the 21 August 2024 Latakia specimen [25]. The May 2022 report is retained separately from the 18 May Banias report [18] because the publications differ in date, reported size, fishing method, position and voucher information; these distinctions support separate reported events, although specimen identity cannot be independently re-examined here. Because the two reports are only three days and approximately 14 km apart, a duplicate cannot be fully excluded; if they were merged, the totals would be 26 entries (13 H. intermedius and 13 H. cf. intermedius) in the same 11 countries. Original coordinates replace several inconsistent derivative positions for Lebanon and Israel [13,14]. The Sorrento observation extends the chronology beyond the regional review. No further source-traceable post-review focal occurrence was recovered in the updated searches.

Coordinate provenance: O, original-paper position or conversion; R, regional-review position; L, locality locator only, not an exact capture coordinate; M, fish-market position, capture locality unknown. NR, not reported or not recovered; TL, total length. The approximately located Gaza has no asserted exact position. The Abbassiya source explicitly describes its coordinates as approximate. The Banias latitude follows the review because the primary latitude string is malformed. The Libyan reports, one by Fitori and Rizgalla [26] and a second photograph published by the Libyan Observer on 26 October 2025, were both reassigned to H. cf. acuminatus in [19] and are excluded [19,26]; their inclusion as originally published would add Libya as a twelfth country and at least one further entry. The Larnaka and Amphora Wall rows of [19], assigned to H. acuminatus and H. cf. acuminatus, are also outside the 27 entries. The 27 entries are reported events; neither entry counts nor displayed coordinate precision establish individual abundance or measurement accuracy.

sec.title: 4.1. Two Conspicuous Tropical Fishes, Contrasting Mediterranean Histories
sec.p: The Mediterranean histories of P. hepatus and H. intermedius differ fundamentally. Paracanthurus hepatus remains exceptionally sparse: substantiated observations are confined to Bat Yam, Corsica and eastern Provence, with no evidence of recruitment, overwintering or a continuous colonization front. By contrast, H. intermedius has been reported repeatedly since its first Mediterranean record in Türkiye in 2002 [12], with a concentration of records in the Levant and additional occurrences in the central Mediterranean and farther west or north [13,14,15,16,17,18,19,20]. This discontinuous pattern contrasts with the progressive dispersal trajectories reconstructed for several non-indigenous Mediterranean fishes [27]. Azzurro et al. (2026) [19] considered the Levantine clustering compatible with an established population and discussed multiple introduction events as an explanation for the wider pattern. Regional establishment status and the origin of isolated outlying occurrences require separate interpretation.

The difference is informative because both fishes are conspicuous and readily detected, yet their record patterns may reflect different combinations of propagule supply, natural connectivity and environmental filtering. For P. hepatus, the shift from isolated single-fish events to at least two individuals in eastern Provence during one summer is noteworthy but still falls far short of establishment. For H. intermedius, repeated eastern Mediterranean observations accumulated over more than two decades and now include multiple photographic, video and voucher-supported records.

sec.title: 4.2. Hypothesized Introduction Pathways and the Relevance of Heniochus acuminatus
sec.p: For P. hepatus, a direct unaided route through the Suez Canal is not supported by its known native distribution, which excludes the Red Sea [4,5,7]. A natural Atlantic source for entry through Gibraltar is likewise absent. Its prominence in the ornamental trade and the occurrence of aquarium-related introductions in the Mediterranean make aquarium release the leading hypothesis [28,29,30,31,32]. Boudouresque et al. [5] specifically proposed accidental or deliberate release from seawater aquaria on board mega-yachts mooring at Saint-Raphaël, a hypothesis that remains untested. However, no release was witnessed for the focal observations. Native-range reasoning identifies plausible pathways; it does not verify the origin or transport history of individual fish, and other human-mediated transport cannot be excluded.

Heniochus intermedius is native to the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, so passage through the Suez Canal and subsequent dispersal offer a plausible explanation for eastern-basin records [12,13,14,19]. Spatially isolated records from Malta, the Adriatic and other central or northern localities have also prompted discussion of shipping and aquarium release [15,19,20]. A discontinuous record map alone cannot establish multiple pathways: it may also reflect incomplete sampling or dispersal between undetected populations. Canal-mediated dispersal, repeated immigration and additional human-assisted introductions therefore remain hypotheses whose relative contributions cannot be resolved with the available occurrence data.

Shipping-related transport warrants consideration for both focal taxa, although its biological plausibility depends on the life stage and transport compartment. Fish transport in ballast water is documented [33]; entrainment of early life stages would be a potential mechanism to examine here. Hull-associated transport could involve mobile fish sheltered in protected vessel compartments, such as sea chests, whose role in organism transfer has been demonstrated [34]. This mechanism is distinct from attachment of sessile fouling organisms to exposed hull surfaces. None of the focal records documents capture in ballast water, occupation of a sea chest or release from a vessel. These possibilities are alternatives for investigation, rather than confirmed explanations or pathways of equal evidential support.

Secondary dispersal from the eastern basin toward the central Mediterranean and Adriatic is biogeographically plausible, but the widely scattered records do not permit reliable inference of a directional route. For example, Malta was reported in 2014, before the Egyptian record of 2017, and the 2024 Adriatic observation preceded the 2025 video records from Cyprus and Crete (Table 1). This sequence describes detection dates, not the order of colonization. The compilation contains no sequence of observations within the Suez Canal that could link these locations. Figure 2 therefore displays occurrence locations without dispersal arrows; neither chronology nor spatial discontinuity establishes the introduction mechanism.

Heniochus acuminatus provides a taxonomic and pathway comparator. Azzurro et al. (2026) [19] documented its first confirmed Mediterranean occurrence from a specimen speared off Larnaka, Cyprus, in August 2018. Its presence demonstrates that superficially similar Heniochus species can reach the basin and reinforces the need for caution when interpreting distant underwater imagery. The Benghazi fish originally published as H. intermedius [26] is excluded from the focal chronology because its assignment to H. cf. acuminatus follows Azzurro et al. (2026) [19], rather than an independent re-examination in this study.

sec.title: 4.3. What Do the New French and Italian Observations Add?
sec.p: The French P. hepatus observation is informative when considered together with the documented removal and observation history. It was approximately 79 m from the site of the fish speared in July and 0.92 km from the position of a second fish last observed on 5 September. It therefore represents either that second fish at a different location or an additional individual. These alternatives imply different individual counts, but the footage and observation gap cannot resolve identity, demonstrate a movement trajectory or quantify local propagule input.

The Sorrento H. cf. intermedius observation post-dates the November 2025 endpoint of the regional Heniochus review [19]. Its reported depth of approximately 8 m and temperature of 27 °C describe the encounter conditions, subject to the unavailable measurement details. A single observation cannot establish residence time, overwintering, direction of movement or introduction pathway. Its contribution is a dated, original-media-supported occurrence with an explicit provisional taxonomic assignment.

The two observations also expose complementary uncertainties. For P. hepatus, the principal problem is individual identity: repeated sightings can overestimate abundance if one fish is counted repeatedly or underestimate propagule pressure if several similar fish are assumed to be one. For H. cf. intermedius, the principal problem is taxonomic confidence from video. Future records should therefore combine full lateral imagery from both sides, exact date and decimal coordinates, depth, habitat and estimated size with individual-recognition features, and should retain vouchers or tissue when legal and practicable. Such metadata allow occurrence, identity and fate to be evaluated separately.

Future molecular studies of both focal species should compare Mediterranean samples with adequate coverage of their native ranges and, where available, ornamental-trade stocks. DNA barcoding can assist identification, whereas evaluating source populations, connectivity and repeated introductions requires informative population markers and representative comparative sampling. Turan and Doğdu [35] used mitochondrial COI and 16S rRNA data for Pterois miles and found patterns consistent with a Red Sea–Indian Ocean source and Suez-mediated entry, while highlighting uneven source-range sampling. Comparable analyses could test origin hypotheses for P. hepatus and H. intermedius without treating a shared barcode alone as proof of a transport route.

sec.title: 4.4. Establishment Potential Under Present and Future Mediterranean Conditions
sec.p: The reviewed evidence does not demonstrate establishment of P. hepatus in the Mediterranean. The documented fish were isolated individuals, and the recovered sources provide no direct evidence of spawning, recruitment, successive locally produced generations or overwintering. Multi-week summer observations in Corsica and Provence indicate short-term persistence. For H. intermedius, establishment should also be considered using the operational approach of the CIESM Atlas [36]. The CIESM listing criteria infer self-maintaining fish populations from at least three published records from different localities or periods [37]. Repeated, taxonomically supported Levantine occurrences meet this criterion and support recognition of H. intermedius as established in the eastern Mediterranean, consistent with previous assessments [14,19]. This operational classification does not require the present study to demonstrate reproduction directly, and it should not be extended to isolated central or northern occurrences. The numerical threshold is an indicator of self-maintenance, rather than an automatic classification of every set of scattered records, including suspected repeated releases of Paracanthurus hepatus.

Environmental suitability and propagule supply can influence establishment, but neither was measured in this study. Winter thermal conditions may constrain a tropical fish such as P. hepatus, while the Red Sea distribution of H. intermedius provides a potential source connected through the Suez corridor. These are biogeographic considerations rather than tests of thermal limits or realized connectivity. Stage-based invasion terminology should be applied to regional populations, distinguishing operational status assessments from direct demographic evidence [38].

Warming may alter survival and establishment opportunities without identifying the introduction pathway. In an AS-ISK screening of 23 alien and neonative Mediterranean fishes, P. hepatus received a Basic Risk Assessment score of 18, classified as medium risk under the calibrated threshold of that study; inclusion of climate-change questions increased the score by 10 points (composite score 28) [39]. Subsequent work advised against ranking species with a composite BRA+CCA threshold [40]. These screening scores are context-dependent risk indicators, not estimates of observed impact or establishment probability. For H. intermedius, the accumulated records and concentration in the Levant should be interpreted against the long-term warming and tropicalization of the Mediterranean, which can facilitate survival and secondary spread of warm-water fishes [41,42,43,44,45].

Warmer conditions may lengthen seasonal survival and increase the probability that future introductions persist long enough to reproduce. Monitoring should therefore focus on repeated local detections, juvenile occurrence and overwintering rather than treating every isolated tropical-fish sighting as evidence of establishment.

sec.title: 4.5. Citizen Science, Early Detection and Evidence Quality
sec.p: For rare and conspicuous fishes, data quality can alter the inferred invasion history as strongly as the number of records. A duplicated observation, an incorrect date, a publication lag or an overconfident species identification can change apparent first occurrences, range limits and propagule count; lag times are a recognized source of bias in reconstructions of Mediterranean fish invasions [10]. National inventories and regional databases likewise demonstrate the value of source-resolved validation for tracking non-indigenous species [46]. Observation effort, geographic coverage, publication delays and identification quality are uneven across sources. Consequently, the chronology and map are descriptive: they do not estimate abundance, occupancy, introduction frequency or a temporal increase in invasion rate. Failure to recover additional records does not demonstrate absence.

Validated public reporting is useful for these conspicuous, shallow-water fishes. AlienFish surveys document its contribution to detecting uncommon and non-indigenous fishes in Italian waters [47], while the Egyptian H. intermedius record emerged from social-media surveillance [17]. The recent Heniochus synthesis similarly draws on photographs and videos provided by sea users [19]. These examples directly relevant to the focal records illustrate the value of retaining original media and validating identifications.

For management, early detection should be linked to pathway-specific action. Aquarium organizations and retailers can communicate surrender alternatives and no-release messaging for unwanted ornamental fishes; marina and port communities can be engaged where shipping or vessel-associated transport is plausible; and citizen networks can rapidly alert specialists when conspicuous newcomers appear.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: The updated Mediterranean occurrence account includes five P. hepatus observation episodes representing at least four individuals and 27 Heniochus entries in 11 countries, comprising 14 retained H. intermedius and 13 provisional H. cf. intermedius assignments. The French fish may be a previously observed individual or an additional fish; the Sorrento taxon remains provisional. The occurrence account distinguishes original source names from the taxonomic treatments adopted from Azzurro et al. (2026) [19]. Aquarium release is the leading pathway hypothesis for P. hepatus, whereas passage through the Suez Canal is plausible for H. intermedius; shipping-related alternatives remain unverified. Verified Levantine records support eastern Mediterranean establishment of H. intermedius under the CIESM operational criterion, without implying establishment at every outlying locality. The scattered records do not permit reliable reconstruction of a directional dispersal route. Continued reporting, demographic observations and comparative genetic sampling can help resolve these questions.
